---
title: "Physics background"
---

Notation used throughout: $f$ = frequency (Hz), $c \approx 343\ \mathrm{m/s}$ =
speed of sound in air at room temperature, $\lambda = c/f$ = wavelength (m),
$V$ = room volume (m³), $T_{60}$ = reverberation time (s), $L_x, L_y, L_z$ =
room dimensions (m), $m$ = partition surface mass (kg/m²), $p$ = acoustic
pressure (Pa), $\rho_0 \approx 1.2\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ = ambient air density,
$\mathbf{u}$ = acoustic particle velocity (m/s), $\omega = 2\pi f$ = angular
frequency (rad/s), $\mathbf{k}$ = wave vector (rad/m) with magnitude
$k = |\mathbf{k}| = \omega/c = 2\pi/\lambda$. Fields are written as complex
amplitudes with time dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, the physical field being
the real part.

For this room $L_x \times L_y \times L_z = 4.445 \times 3.658 \times
2.692\ \mathrm{m}$ ($V = 43.8\ \mathrm{m^3}$), with the origin at the S1
corner on the floor as on the [layout](layout.qmd) page.

## Sound as a pressure field

### Linear acoustics

At the levels of interest (the drone is roughly 60–70 dB SPL, i.e.
$|p| \sim 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ against an ambient
$p_0 \approx 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$) air is an ideal linear medium. Linearizing
the Euler and continuity equations about rest, with adiabatic compression
$p = c^2 \rho'$ ($\rho'$ = density perturbation), gives

$$
\rho_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} = -\nabla p,
\qquad
\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} + \rho_0 \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}
= \rho_0\, q(\mathbf{r}, t),
$$

where $q$ (s⁻¹) is the volume-velocity source density: the rate at which a
source (a loudspeaker cone, or a vibrating wall) injects volume, per unit
volume. Eliminating $\mathbf{u}$ yields the inhomogeneous wave equation,
and at a single frequency the **Helmholtz equation**:

$$
\nabla^2 p - \frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial t^2}
= -\rho_0 \frac{\partial q}{\partial t}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\left(\nabla^2 + k^2\right) p(\mathbf{r}) = i\omega\rho_0\, q(\mathbf{r}).
$$

Two facts here carry the whole project. First, the equation is **linear**,
so the field of several sources is the sum of their fields: a loudspeaker
field equal and opposite to the drone's field at some set of points
cancels it there exactly. That is all ANC is. Second, pressure is a
**scalar** field: one microphone measures all of it at a point, and
cancellation means matching one complex number per point per frequency.

### Plane waves and the wave vector

In free space the source-free equation is solved by plane waves

$$
p(\mathbf{r}, t) = P\, e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} - \omega t)},
\qquad |\mathbf{k}| = \frac{\omega}{c},
$$

with complex amplitude $P$. The dispersion relation is linear and
isotropic (air is non-dispersive at these frequencies), so $\mathbf{k}$ is
free in direction but fixed in magnitude: at 59 Hz,
$k = 1.08\ \mathrm{rad/m}$ and $\lambda = 5.8\ \mathrm{m}$, longer than
any dimension of the room. Euler's equation then gives the particle
velocity

$$
\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{\rho_0\,\omega}\, p
= \frac{\hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\rho_0 c}\, p,
$$

parallel to $\mathbf{k}$ (sound is longitudinal) and in phase with $p$ for
a single travelling wave; $\rho_0 c \approx 412\ \mathrm{Pa\,s/m}$ is the
characteristic impedance of air. The time-averaged intensity (power flux)
is $\mathbf{I} = |P|^2 \hat{\mathbf{k}} / (2\rho_0 c)$.

Any single-frequency field in a source-free region can be written as a
superposition of plane waves with $|\mathbf{k}| = \omega/c$ (an angular
spectrum). In k-space such a field therefore lives on the sphere of radius
$\omega/c$, and that sphere is the object to keep in mind for what follows.

### Standing waves and the boundary condition

The walls, floor and ceiling are, to a first approximation, rigid: the
normal particle velocity vanishes there, so by Euler's equation
$\partial p / \partial n = 0$ (a Neumann condition). Two counter-propagating
plane waves along $x$, $e^{ik_x x} + e^{-ik_x x} = 2\cos k_x x$, have
$\partial_x p \propto \sin k_x x$, which vanishes at $x = 0$; it also
vanishes at $x = L_x$ only if

$$
k_x = \frac{n_x \pi}{L_x}, \qquad n_x = 0, 1, 2, \dots
$$

Rigid walls are therefore **pressure antinodes** and **velocity nodes**.
The particle velocity of the standing wave, $u_x \propto \sin k_x x$, is
$90°$ out of phase with $p$ and peaks a quarter wavelength from the wall,
which is the origin of the passive-absorber argument
[below](#why-passive-absorption-fails-at-low-frequency).

## Room modes

### Modes as a lattice in k-space

Imposing the condition on all three axes gives the eigenfunctions (mode
shapes) and eigenfrequencies of the rectangular room,

$$
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) = \cos\frac{n_x\pi x}{L_x}\,
\cos\frac{n_y\pi y}{L_y}\,\cos\frac{n_z\pi z}{L_z},
\qquad
\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{n}} = \pi\left(\frac{n_x}{L_x}, \frac{n_y}{L_y},
\frac{n_z}{L_z}\right),
\qquad
f_{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{c\,|\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{n}}|}{2\pi},
$$

labelled by the non-negative integer triple $\mathbf{n} = (n_x, n_y, n_z)$.
Expanding each cosine into exponentials shows what a mode is physically:

$$
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{8}
\sum_{\pm,\pm,\pm} e^{\,i(\pm k_x x \pm k_y y \pm k_z z)},
$$

a superposition of the plane waves whose wave vectors are the mirror images
$(\pm k_x, \pm k_y, \pm k_z)$ of $\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{n}}$, bouncing between
the walls. An **axial** mode (one nonzero index) is 2 distinct plane waves
travelling along one axis, a **tangential** mode (two nonzero) is 4 waves in
a plane, and an **oblique** mode (three nonzero) is 8 waves. The boundary
condition has turned the continuous sphere of allowed $\mathbf{k}$ into a
rectangular lattice with spacings $\pi/L_x$, $\pi/L_y$, $\pi/L_z$. It is
the same mathematics as a particle in a box, with Neumann rather than
Dirichlet walls (so index 0 is allowed).

![The $(k_x, k_y)$ plane of the room's mode lattice (the same in-plane
lattice repeats for each $n_z$). A drive at frequency $f$ sits on the shell
$|\mathbf{k}| = 2\pi f/c$; modes whose lattice points lie near that shell
respond resonantly. For $n_z = 1$ the shell's in-plane radius shrinks to
$\sqrt{k^2 - (\pi/L_z)^2}$, which is real only above
$f_{001} = 63.7$ Hz, so at 39.9 and 59 Hz only $n_z = 0$ modes lie inside
the shell. Generated by
[`scripts/physics_figures.py`](https://github.com/madi-lts/roomANC/blob/master/scripts/physics_figures.py).](images/k-lattice.png){#fig-k-lattice}

Reading @fig-k-lattice: the 39.9 Hz shell passes almost through (1,0,·),
so at that tone the room is essentially one axial mode; the 59 Hz shell
lies between (1,1,0) at 60.7 Hz and the vertical axial (0,0,1) at 63.7 Hz
(off this plane, not drawn); the 120 Hz shells thread a cluster of four
modes. The full mode table is on the [Modes](modes.qmd) page.

### Mode counting and the modal regime

Each lattice point occupies a k-space volume $\pi^3/V$, so the number of
modes below $f$ is, to leading order, the volume of the sphere's positive
octant divided by that cell volume (Weyl's law). Surface and edge
corrections enter because the lattice includes its boundary planes
($n_i = 0$):

$$
N(f) \approx \frac{4\pi V f^3}{3c^3} + \frac{\pi S f^2}{4c^2}
+ \frac{L f}{8c},
$$

where $S = 2(L_xL_y + L_yL_z + L_zL_x) = 76.1\ \mathrm{m^2}$ is the total
surface area and $L = 4(L_x + L_y + L_z) = 43.2\ \mathrm{m}$ the total edge
length. For this room $N(150\ \mathrm{Hz}) \approx 29$, matching the exact
count of 29 on the [Modes](modes.qmd) page, and only 2 modes lie below
60 Hz. The density $dN/df$ grows as $f^2$; once the spacing between
neighbouring modes falls below their bandwidth $\Delta f$ the modes overlap
and the individual lattice points stop mattering. That crossover is the
Schroeder frequency of the [next section](#modal-vs-diffuse-regime).

### Pressure in a mode: antinodes, nodes and orthogonality

Three properties of $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$ are used throughout the site:

- **Corners are universal antinodes.** At any corner every cosine is
  $\pm 1$, so $|\psi_{\mathbf{n}}| = 1$ for every mode. Corners (and, more
  weakly, edges and walls) are where the room is loudest.
- **Parity and nodal planes.** Reflection through the mid-plane
  $x \to L_x - x$ multiplies $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$ by $(-1)^{n_x}$. Every mode
  with odd $n_x$ is therefore odd about $x = L_x/2$ and vanishes on that
  whole plane; likewise for $y$ and $z$. The mid-planes are the most
  important nodal surfaces in the room because they belong to all of the
  lowest modes.
- **Orthogonality.** $\int_V \psi_{\mathbf{m}} \psi_{\mathbf{n}}\, dV =
  \Lambda_{\mathbf{n}} V \delta_{\mathbf{mn}}$ with
  $\Lambda_{\mathbf{n}} = \prod_i \varepsilon_{n_i}$, where
  $\varepsilon_0 = 1$ and $\varepsilon_{n>0} = 1/2$. Any pressure field in
  the room can be expanded as $p = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} A_{\mathbf{n}}
  \psi_{\mathbf{n}}$, and its time-averaged acoustic potential energy is a
  sum over modes, $E_p = \frac{V}{4\rho_0c^2} \sum_{\mathbf{n}}
  \Lambda_{\mathbf{n}} |A_{\mathbf{n}}|^2$. This is the precise sense in
  which cancelling a mode is a global statement about the room.


## Modal vs. diffuse regime {#modal-vs-diffuse-regime}

The character of a room's sound field changes at the **Schroeder frequency**

$$
f_S \approx 2000 \sqrt{\frac{T_{60}}{V}},
$$

with $T_{60}$ in seconds and $V$ in m³. For $V \approx 50\ \mathrm{m^3}$ and
$T_{60} \approx 0.4\ \mathrm{s}$, $f_S \approx 180\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

- **Below $f_S$ (modal regime):** the field is a superposition of a small
  number of discrete room modes with low modal overlap. The response at any
  point is dominated by a few modes, so driving those modes in antiphase with
  a few loudspeakers cancels the field **globally** — the whole room gets
  quieter, not just the neighborhood of an error microphone.
- **Above $f_S$ (diffuse regime):** modal density and overlap are high; the
  field at two points separated by more than $\sim\lambda/2$ decorrelates.
  ANC then produces only a quiet zone of radius $\sim\lambda/10$ around each
  error microphone — at 1 kHz that is ~3 cm. Not viable for a room.

The HVAC drone consists of a few stable tones below ~150 Hz, safely inside
the modal regime. This is the single most important fact about the project:
**global cancellation is physically available here**, with an expected
10–20 dB reduction at the tones across most of the room and little effect on
broadband content. Car-cabin engine-order cancellation is the commercial
precedent for exactly this configuration.

## Driving the room: point sources and mode coupling

### The modal Green's function

A subwoofer at $\lambda \approx 3$–$9\ \mathrm{m}$ is acoustically a point
monopole: its cabinet is much smaller than a wavelength, so it is a volume
velocity $Q_s$ (m³/s) injected at its position $\mathbf{r}_s$,
$q = Q_s\, \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s)$. Expanding
$p = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} A_{\mathbf{n}} \psi_{\mathbf{n}}$ in the Helmholtz
equation, using $\nabla^2 \psi_{\mathbf{n}} = -k_{\mathbf{n}}^2
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$, and projecting onto $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$ with the
orthogonality relation gives each modal amplitude:

$$
A_{\mathbf{n}} = G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)\, \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)\, Q_s,
\qquad
G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega) \equiv \frac{-i\omega\rho_0}
{\Lambda_{\mathbf{n}} V\left(k_{\mathbf{n}}^2 - k^2 - i\,k\,k_{\mathbf{n}}/\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{n}}\right)},
$$

so that the pressure at a receiver $\mathbf{r}$ is

$$
p(\mathbf{r}) = Q_s \sum_{\mathbf{n}}
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r})\, G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)\,
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s).
$$

Here $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{n}} = f_{\mathbf{n}}/\Delta f$ is the modal quality factor
(written $\mathcal{Q}$ to keep it apart from the volume velocity $Q_s$;
wall and furnishing losses, added phenomenologically; with the assumed
$T_{60} = 0.4$ s, $\Delta f \approx 5.5$ Hz and $\mathcal{Q} \approx 7$–$27$ across
the band), $G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)$ is the modal response (the
amplitude of mode $\mathbf{n}$ per unit volume velocity injected at an
antinode), and the sum is the same damped modal sum the
[Modes](modes.qmd#model) page evaluates numerically.

The section title is literal: $G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)$ is the
$\mathbf{n}$-th coefficient of the room's Green's function, up to the
source-strength factor. Define the **Green's function**
$G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_s)$ of the Helmholtz operator with rigid
(Neumann) walls as the solution of

$$
\left(\nabla^2 + k^2\right) G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_s)
= -\,\delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s),
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla G = 0 \ \text{on the walls},
$$

with $\delta$ the three-dimensional Dirac distribution and
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ the wall normal. Expanding $G$ in the eigenfunctions
$\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$ (the bilinear, or spectral, representation — the same
diagonalization used for any normal operator) and projecting with the
orthogonality relation gives

$$
G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_s) = \sum_{\mathbf{n}}
\frac{\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r})\,\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)}
{\Lambda_{\mathbf{n}}\, V \left(k_{\mathbf{n}}^2 - k^2\right)}.
$$

The monopole enters the Helmholtz equation as
$(\nabla^2 + k^2)\, p = i\omega\rho_0\, Q_s\,
\delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s)$, so
$p(\mathbf{r}) = -\,i\omega\rho_0\, Q_s\, G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_s)$,
and comparing term by term with the modal sum above:

$$
G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega) = -\,i\omega\rho_0 \times
\frac{1}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{n}}\, V \left(k_{\mathbf{n}}^2 - k^2\right)},
$$

i.e. $G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)$ is $-i\omega\rho_0$ times the bare spectral
coefficient of $G$. The factor $-i\omega\rho_0$ converts source strength
(volume velocity) into pressure, making
$p/Q_s = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r})\,
G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)\, \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)$ a transfer
**impedance** (Pa per m³/s) rather than the kernel of
$(\nabla^2 + k^2)^{-1}$ itself. Damping enters by the phenomenological
pole shift $k_{\mathbf{n}}^2 \to k_{\mathbf{n}}^2 -
i\,k\,k_{\mathbf{n}}/\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{n}}$, which moves each modal pole
off the real-$\omega$ axis (the lossy room has quasi-modes with finite
linewidth $\Delta f = f_{\mathbf{n}}/\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{n}}$); that
substitution in the expression above reproduces the definition of
$G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)$ given at the top of this section. The symmetry of
$G$ under $\mathbf{r} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{r}_s$ is the acoustic
reciprocity theorem — item 3 below.

Three things follow directly from this form.

1. **Coupling is the mode shape at the source.** Mode $\mathbf{n}$ is
   excited in proportion to $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)$. This is the
   same selection rule as an atom in a cavity, whose coupling to a cavity
   mode is $g(\mathbf{r}) \propto \psi(\mathbf{r}_{\text{atom}})$: placed on
   a node, it does not see that mode however well tuned.
2. **Tuning supplies gain, position supplies access.** Driving at
   $\omega \to \omega_{\mathbf{n}}$ enhances mode $\mathbf{n}$ by roughly
   $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{n}}$ over its off-resonant neighbours, so a source does
   preferentially drive the mode it is tuned to, provided
   $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s) \neq 0$. With $\mathcal{Q} \sim 10$ the
   selectivity is modest: at 59 Hz both (1,1,0) (1.7 Hz away) and (0,0,1)
   (4.7 Hz away) sit within one bandwidth, plus an off-resonant background
   from every other mode.
3. **Reciprocity.** The kernel is symmetric in $\mathbf{r}$ and
   $\mathbf{r}_s$. Swapping source and receiver gives the same transfer
   function, so a microphone *observes* mode $\mathbf{n}$ in proportion to
   $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_{\text{mic}})$ by exactly the argument that
   makes a speaker *drive* it in proportion to $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)$.
   The secondary paths the controller identifies (speaker $s$ to mic $m$)
   are $H_{ms}(\omega) = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_m)\,
   G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)\, \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)$: the geometry of the
   speakers and of the mics enter symmetrically, which is why the
   [observability analysis](modes.qmd#observability-of-the-6-mic-array) of
   the mics and the placement of the subs use the same matrix of
   $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$ values.

### Where a source can and cannot couple

![Floor-plane mode shapes for one mode under each target tone.
Dashed lines: nodal lines. Squares: subwoofer corners S1–S4 (filled = the
current diagonal pair). Diamonds: mid-wall points and the floor centre.
Stars: pillow points. A source on a dashed line cannot drive that mode;
every corner sits on $|\psi| = 1$ of every mode.](images/mode-coupling.png){#fig-mode-coupling}

The parity rule makes the candidate positions easy to score. A point on
the mid-plane $x = L_x/2$ cannot drive any odd-$n_x$ mode, and a mid-wall
or floor-centre point lies on **two** such mid-planes. The couplings
$\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)$ for the modes nearest the target tones:

| Mode | $f_{\mathbf{n}}$ (Hz) | Near tone | Corner | Mid-wall $x=0$ $(0, \tfrac{L_y}{2}, \tfrac{L_z}{2})$ | Mid-wall $y=0$ $(\tfrac{L_x}{2}, 0, \tfrac{L_z}{2})$ | Floor centre $(\tfrac{L_x}{2}, \tfrac{L_y}{2}, 0)$ | Pillows |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| (1,0,0) | 38.6 | 39.9 | ±1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | −0.40, −0.74 |
| (0,1,0) | 46.9 | — | ±1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | −0.96, −0.96 |
| (1,1,0) | 60.7 | 59.0 | ±1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.38, 0.71 |
| (0,0,1) | 63.7 | 59.0 | ±1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0.73, 0.73 |
| (3,0,0) | 115.7 | 117.9 | ±1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0.94, 0.60 |
| (1,2,1) | 119.7 | 120.0 | ±1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | −0.24, −0.44 |
| (2,2,0) | 121.4 | 120.0 | ±1 | −1 | −1 | 1 | −0.57, 0.08 |

(Pillow points $(2.80, 3.31, 0.65)$ and $(3.40, 3.31, 0.65)$ m.) Because
every coordinate of the mid-wall and centre points is $0$ or $L/2$, their
couplings are exactly $0$ or $\pm 1$: a mid-wall source is a clean
single-axis drive at the lowest frequencies, but every mode with **two or
more odd indices** is invisible to all three of them. That includes
(1,1,0), the resonance under the 59 Hz drone, and (1,2,1) at 120 Hz, both
of which are loud at the pillows. A set of mid-wall and centre subs
therefore cannot control the drone at all through its dominant mode,
whatever their number or tuning.

A corner couples to everything, and the real cabinets, pushed into the
corners with their centres about 0.35 m from each wall and the driver
near the floor, keep $|\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)| \geq 0.9$ for the
four modes below 65 Hz and $\geq 0.6$ for every mode to 150 Hz. That is
the physical basis of corner loading on the [Layout](layout.qmd) page.

### The control equation

Everything above was for one source. ANC is the same algebra with two
kinds of source in the room at once, and it is worth setting out with
every symbol defined, because the controller, the sub placement and the
mic placement all live in this one equation.

**Primary and secondary fields.** The *primary* field is the drone as it
is now: pressure radiated into the room by the HVAC plant through the
walls, floor and ducts, described by an unknown, distributed source
density $q_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{r})$. The subscript $\mathrm{p}$ (upright)
labels "primary" throughout; it is not the pressure $p$. The *secondary*
field is what the $N_s$ subwoofers add, sub $s = 1, \dots, N_s$ injecting
the complex volume velocity $Q_s$ (m³/s) at $\mathbf{r}_s$. By linearity
the total pressure is the sum, and each part has its own modal expansion
in the same basis $\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$:

$$
p(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \Big( A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}}
+ A_{\mathrm{s},\mathbf{n}} \Big)\, \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}).
$$

Here $A_{\mathbf{n}}$ is, as before, the complex amplitude (Pa) of mode
$\mathbf{n}$ in the expansion $p = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} A_{\mathbf{n}}
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}$, at the single tone frequency $\omega$ under
consideration; $A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}}$ is the part produced by the
drone and $A_{\mathrm{s},\mathbf{n}}$ the part produced by the subs.

**Primary amplitudes.** Projecting the Helmholtz equation with the
distributed source $q_{\mathrm{p}}$ exactly as for the point source gives

$$
A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}} = G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)
\int_V \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r})\, q_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{r})\, dV .
$$

The overlap integral is how strongly the drone's source distribution
projects onto mode $\mathbf{n}$. We never know $q_{\mathrm{p}}$, so the
$A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}}$ are unknown, but at fixed $\omega$ they are
just fixed complex numbers, one per mode, and slowly varying as the plant
drifts. The overlap integral is what the [Modes](modes.qmd#model) page
sets to an equal $a_{\mathbf{n}} = 1$ for every mode, and what the baseline
measurement campaign will constrain.

**Secondary amplitudes and the coupling matrix.** Summing the point-source
result over subs,

$$
A_{\mathrm{s},\mathbf{n}} = \sum_{s=1}^{N_s} B_{\mathbf{n}s}\, Q_s,
\qquad
B_{\mathbf{n}s} \equiv G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)\,
\psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s).
$$

$B_{\mathbf{n}s}$ (Pa per m³/s) is the amplitude sub $s$ puts into mode
$\mathbf{n}$ per unit volume velocity. It factors into a frequency part
$G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)$ that depends only on the room and a geometric part
$\Phi_{\mathbf{n}s} \equiv \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_s)$ that depends
only on where the sub is: $B = G\,\Phi$ with
$G = \operatorname{diag}\big(G_{\mathbf{n}}(\omega)\big)$.

**Cancellation.** Keep the set $\mathcal{M}$ of the $M$ modes that matter
at the tone (the near-resonant ones; more if the target is a small region
where off-resonant modes add up). Cancelling them means making every total
modal amplitude in $\mathcal{M}$ vanish:

$$
\boxed{\;A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}} + \sum_{s=1}^{N_s}
B_{\mathbf{n}s}\, Q_s = 0, \qquad \mathbf{n} \in \mathcal{M}\;}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}} + B\,\mathbf{Q} = 0,
$$

with $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}} \in \mathbb{C}^{M}$ the primary amplitudes,
$\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{C}^{N_s}$ the sub volume velocities, and
$B \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N_s}$. That is $M$ complex linear equations in
$N_s$ complex unknowns, and the usual three cases apply.

- $N_s = M$: a unique solution $\mathbf{Q} = -B^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}}$
  if and only if $\det B \neq 0$. Since every $G_{\mathbf{n}} \neq 0$,
  $\det B = \det G \cdot \det \Phi$, so **whether the modes can be
  controlled is purely geometric**: it is decided by $\det\Phi$, the
  mode shapes at the sub positions, and no amount of tuning or gain
  changes it.
- $N_s < M$: overdetermined. The best the subs can do is minimize the
  residual acoustic potential energy, which by orthogonality is
  $J = \sum_{\mathbf{n} \in \mathcal{M}} \Lambda_{\mathbf{n}}
  \big| A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}} + \sum_s B_{\mathbf{n}s} Q_s \big|^2$
  (up to the constant $V/4\rho_0c^2$). Setting
  $\partial J / \partial Q_s^* = 0$ gives, in index and matrix form,
  $$
  \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \Lambda_{\mathbf{n}} B^*_{\mathbf{n}s}
  \Big( A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}} + \sum_{s'} B_{\mathbf{n}s'} Q_{s'} \Big) = 0
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{opt}} = -\big(B^\dagger \Lambda B\big)^{-1}
  B^\dagger \Lambda\, \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}},
  $$
  with $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\Lambda_{\mathbf{n}})$ and $\dagger$
  the conjugate transpose. The part of $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}}$ outside
  the column space of $B$ is left untouched.
- $N_s > M$: underdetermined, a family of solutions; the controller can
  spend the extra freedom on minimum drive effort $\|\mathbf{Q}\|^2$ or on
  cancelling more modes.

**Conditioning.** Write the singular value decomposition of the weighted
coupling matrix, $\Lambda^{1/2} B = \sum_k \sigma_k\,
\mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{v}_k^\dagger$, with singular values $\sigma_k$ and
orthonormal left and right singular vectors $\mathbf{u}_k$ (mode space)
and $\mathbf{v}_k$ (sub space). The optimal drive is

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{opt}} = -\sum_k \frac{\mathbf{u}_k^\dagger
\Lambda^{1/2} \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\sigma_k}\, \mathbf{v}_k ,
$$

so the component of the primary field along a weakly coupled direction
$\mathbf{u}_k$ costs drive $\propto 1/\sigma_k$. A small $\sigma_{\min}$
means large sub excursions, and it also amplifies errors: if the
controller's model of $B$ is off by a relative error $\delta$ (a gain or
phase drift after secondary-path identification), the residual is of
order $\delta\,|\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}}|$, which caps the suppression at
roughly $-20\log_{10}\delta$ (a 1 dB gain error, $\delta \approx 0.12$,
caps it near 18 dB), and the cap tightens along directions with small
$\sigma_k$. So the requirement on placement is not just
$\operatorname{rank} B = M$ but a well-conditioned $B$: at least $M$ subs,
each off the nodal surfaces of the modes in $\mathcal{M}$, with
**linearly independent coupling vectors**. More subs buy independent
control and conditioning, not reach: a sub with zero coupling to a mode
adds nothing for it.

**What the controller actually sees.** The controller never measures
$A_{\mathbf{n}}$; it sees the pressures $e_m$ at the error mics
$m = 1, \dots, N_m$, at $\mathbf{r}_m$. Evaluating the total field there,
with $\Psi_{m\mathbf{n}} \equiv \psi_{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}_m)$ the
observability matrix of the [Modes](modes.qmd#observability-of-the-6-mic-array)
page,

$$
e_m = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \Psi_{m\mathbf{n}} \Big( A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}}
+ \sum_s B_{\mathbf{n}s} Q_s \Big)
= d_m + \sum_s H_{ms}\, Q_s,
\qquad
\mathbf{e} = \Psi\big(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}} + B\,\mathbf{Q}\big),
$$

where $d_m = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \Psi_{m\mathbf{n}} A_{\mathrm{p},\mathbf{n}}$
is the drone as heard at mic $m$ and
$H_{ms} = \sum_{\mathbf{n}} \Psi_{m\mathbf{n}} B_{\mathbf{n}s}$ is the
secondary path from sub $s$ to mic $m$, the quantity identified in
secondary-path ID. (In hardware the controller sets a drive voltage, not
$Q_s$; the amplifier and driver response just multiply column $s$ and are
absorbed into the identified $H_{ms}$.) The multichannel FxLMS controller
of the [spec](spec.qmd) adapts $\mathbf{Q}$ to minimize
$\sum_m |e_m|^2$. If $\Psi$ has full column rank on $\mathcal{M}$, then
$\mathbf{e} = 0$ forces $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{p}} + B\mathbf{Q} = 0$ on
$\mathcal{M}$: driving the mics to zero is the same as cancelling the
modes. So the two placement problems are the two factors of one product:
**the subs set $B$ (controllability), the mics set $\Psi$
(observability)**, and the cancellation is only as good as the worse of
the two.

### Example: the diagonal sub pair

Symmetric source placements can fail the independence test even at
corners. The corner couplings differ only in sign, $(-1)^{n_x i_x + n_y i_y
+ n_z i_z}$ for the corner at $(i_x L_x, i_y L_y, i_z L_z)$, and the two
floor corners of a diagonal pair, S1 at $(0,0)$ and S4 at $(L_x, L_y)$,
have identical signs for every mode with $n_x + n_y$ even. At 59 Hz that
is **both** (1,1,0) and (0,0,1), so their coupling vectors restricted to
those two modes are parallel: the diagonal pair can null whichever
combination the primary field presents at two chosen points (it has the
off-resonant (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) as a lever, which it drives
differentially), but it cannot set the two dominant 59 Hz modes
independently over the whole room. An adjacent pair (S1 + S2 or S1 + S3)
has opposite signs on (1,1,0) and equal signs on (0,0,1), so it spans
both; so does any three or four corners. Explicitly, on
$\mathcal{M} = \{(1,1,0), (0,0,1)\}$ and with the cabinet couplings
$a = \psi_{110}(\mathbf{r}_{S1}) \approx 0.93$ and
$b = \psi_{001}(\mathbf{r}_{S1}) \approx 0.94$,

$$
\Phi_{\text{S1,S4}} = \begin{pmatrix} a & a \\ b & b \end{pmatrix},
\quad \det = 0;
\qquad
\Phi_{\text{S1,S2}} = \begin{pmatrix} a & -a \\ b & b \end{pmatrix},
\quad \det = 2ab \approx 1.7 .
$$

### Where the room is loud, and where the bed sits

The same mode shapes say where the listener is. The bed head is against a
wall, i.e. on a pressure antinode of every mode with $n_y \geq 1$, and the
pillow columns of the table above are correspondingly large. Moving the
head toward a mid-plane removes the odd modes along that axis passively
(the [recommended bed placement](modes.qmd#recommended-bed-placement)
exploits $x \approx L_x/2$ against (1,0,0) and (1,1,0)); what remains, such
as (0,0,1) whose nodal plane is at $z = L_z/2 = 1.35$ m, is what the
actuators must handle, and the measured level-vs-position map is the
ground truth that pins down the real nodal surfaces.

## Why passive absorption fails at low frequency

Porous absorbers (foam, rockwool panels) dissipate energy via viscous drag,
which requires **particle velocity**. At a rigid wall the normal particle
velocity is zero; it peaks a quarter wavelength away, $\lambda/4 \approx
1.4\ \mathrm{m}$ at 60 Hz. A 5 cm foam panel on a wall sits in a velocity
null nearly the full spectrum below 150 Hz — it does essentially nothing.

What does work passively, with caveats:

- **Deep corner traps**: 60–100 cm of rockwool spanning a corner reaches into
  the velocity field and damps modes (lowers their quality factor $\mathcal{Q}$).
- **Tuned resonant absorbers** (Helmholtz or membrane), tuned to the drone
  tone. These are narrowband and are defeated by pitch drift of the source.

Lowering modal $\mathcal{Q}$ does not remove the tone, but it makes the plant gentler
and the ANC loop easier to stabilize — **passive damping and active control
are complementary**, not alternatives.

## Why passive blocking is weak

Transmission loss of a single-leaf partition follows the **mass law**,

$$
\mathrm{TL} \approx 20 \log_{10}(f \cdot m) - 47\ \mathrm{dB},
$$

with $f$ in Hz and $m$ in kg/m². At 60 Hz even a heavy wall transmits well,
and in practice **leaks dominate**: window frames, outlets, penetrations.
The cheap, rental-compatible airborne fixes are acoustic caulk, mass-loaded
vinyl over the window, and door weatherstripping — worthwhile, but they
cannot reach the tens of dB needed on their own.

## Structure-borne path

Vibration transmitted through the slab and framing is re-radiated by the
room's own surfaces. This path **bypasses every in-room airborne treatment**
(blocking and absorption alike).

**Diagnostic:** open a window. If the drone level barely changes, the
dominant path is structure-borne, and the real fix is isolation at the
source (landlord track: spring/elastomer mounts under the rooftop units and
pumps). ANC still works against the re-radiated field regardless of the
path, because it cancels the in-room pressure directly — another reason it
is the primary mitigation here.
